report.answer: No. Once it leaves the astronaut's hands the globe drifts in a straight line at constant speed — about 0.43 m/s in the 1.0-2.0 s toss. A projectile fit to that free flight gives an effective downward acceleration of only 0.024 ± 0.008 m/s², essentially zero compared to Earth's 9.81 m/s², and over the whole 8 s constant-velocity beats any accelerated law. That is free-fall in orbit — weightlessness, not a push.
assumptions: Camera is still and motion is roughly in a plane facing the camera.
Scale from the globe itself, assumed 0.30 ± 0.08 m diameter, at same depth as motion.
Fit 30-59 is true free flight between hand contacts.

forks.label: Same toss on Earth
forks.why: With 9.81 m/s² the 0.43 m/s toss would arc and drop ~0.5 m in 0.3 s instead of floating straight.

forks.label: Same toss on the Moon
forks.why: With 1.62 m/s² the straight drift would become a slow visible arc, ~70x larger fall than measured.
